They asked him how he could do that and he told them that he would show them. He took off his bow and arrows and stuck them into the ground and then he lay down beside them.
Then he closed his eyes and when he was asleep the young men saw that his body began to shine and a bright light came from him. Then they heard a loud noise like thunder and they saw that Wah-to-yu-hay had gone up into the sky.
The young men were very afraid and they didn't know what to do. Then they heard a voice that said, "Fear not; this is a good thing that Wah-to-yu-hay has done. He has become a Thunderbird and he will help us in our hunting and he will make the weather good for our farming. Now go home and I will tell you more about this."
The voice belonged to the chief of all the spirits and from then on the two young men never had any trouble on their hunts and their village prospered. And every time there was a thunderstorm they knew that Wah-to-yu-hay was making the weather good for them.

While they were there an eclipse of the moon took place and the two men were astonished by it. Then they heard a voice, which they thought was from an old man, talking to them. The voice told them that they were in danger and that they should go to the sandbar. They went to the sandbar and found an old man sitting there. The old man told them that he had been sent by the Great Spirit to help them. He then prophesied the coming of white men and the destruction of Indian culture. He told them that they should go to a certain hill and there they would find a pipe which had been left by the Great Spirit. The pipe would help them to know what to do in the coming days. The two young men went to the hill and found the pipe as the old man had said. They took the pipe and placed it in their village.
The story is similar to some other Native American prophecy narratives, such as the prophecy of the Ghost Dance and the prophecy of Handsome Lake, in that it involves a prophecy of the coming of white men and the destruction of Indian culture, and the discovery of a sacred pipe that will help Native Americans in the coming days.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roar of a bear, then another and another, and soon all hell was breaking loose. The two young men ran for their canoe and their lives, shoving off just as a huge wave engulfed their camp. They paddled for their lives as the volcano Mount Mazama exploded, sending a cloud of ash 44 miles high.  They were covered in ash when they reached safety on the north shore of the lake that is now called Crater Lake.

The story is told by the Klamath people, the indigenous people of the area.  Mount Mazama is 7,257 feet high and is the highest point in the Cascade Range in Oregon.  The eruption of Mount Mazama occurred approximately 6,870 years ago (5,630 BP), ± 150 years.  The eruption of Mount Mazama created the fifth youngest lake in the world, Crater Lake.  The lake is 1,943 feet deep and is the deepest lake in the United States. 
The Klamath people believe that the eruption of Mount Mazama was due to the actions of two young men.  The young men were out on the lake hunting seals when they heard a strange roaring noise.  They saw a large island in the middle of the lake that was covered in fire.  The men were afraid and begged for forgiveness for any wrongs they may have committed.  The fire and the roaring noise continued for two days and then finally stopped.  The next day the island was covered in water and a cloud of ash rose into the sky.  The Klamath people believe that the island is now the place where the volcano erupted, which is now called Wizard Island.

Analysis
This myth is from the Kwakiutl of the northwest coast of North America. It is a myth about spirits of the waters. The story begins with two young men going down to the river to hunt seals. They hear a strange noise and go to investigate. They try to communicate with the source of the sound but receive no answer. They take a stick and mark the spot and then go home. When they return the next day they are unable to find the spot where they left the stick. The story ends there.

Interpretation
The story has been interpreted as a creation myth. The two young men represent two brothers who go out into the world to hunt for food and shelter. They encounter the spirits of the waters which represent the forces of nature. The spirits make strange noises which the men do not understand. The men try to communicate with the spirits but receive no answer. They leave a mark and go home. When they return the next day they are unable to find the mark. This represents the fact that the forces of nature are beyond human comprehension and cannot be controlled by humans.

The story was written down in the 1930s by George Mercer Dawson, a Canadian ethnologist. The place name Egulac is a phonetic spelling of the name as it was pronounced for Dawson by a Cree informant. The name is thought to be derived from a Cree phrase meaning "place of the alders." The story is set in a vague past, but "one night two young men from Egulac" is the opening line.
The story is usually told without the introduction. The opening line is enough to identify the story and introduce the setting. The story is often told in a question-and-answer format. The question and answer are usually spoken by different characters, with the question spoken by the narrator and the answer by an old man or a Cree informant. They heard a sound like the hum of a swarm of bees, and then a great light appeared and two spirits came down the river in a canoe. The spirits introduced themselves as Coyote and Kingfisher, and said they had come to take the two young men with them. The young men refused, and Coyote offered to give them anything they wanted if they would come with him. The men again refused, and Coyote said that he would give the first thing that came to mind when he returned to the river. He went away, and when he returned he had a salmon in his mouth. Then he went away again and when he returned he had a deer in his mouth. Then he went away once more and when he returned he had a beautiful woman in his mouth. He offered this woman to each of the young men in turn, but they both refused her because they had wives. Coyote then went away for the third time and when he returned he was alone. He said to the young men, "I have kept my word. What do you want now?" They said they wanted to go home. Coyote put them into his canoe and pushed them to shore with his canoe paddle. When they were safely on land he said to them, "I will give you a clue to where I am going. I am going to the place where the trees have bark, where there are no birds and no fish, where there is nothing but sticks and stones." The young men understood that he was going to the place of death, and they knew that there he would change his form and become a dog.

The story in mythological terms
The story is told from the perspective of two young hunters. The events in the story can be seen as a metaphorical description of the hero's journey. The two young men start off on their journey, going down to the river to hunt seals. The fog and calm can be seen as a threshold, separating the ordinary world from the supernatural world.
The voices they hear can be seen as the call to adventure. The fact that they hear their own voices answering can be seen as the inner voice that must be listened to in order to embark on the journey. The voices are coming from the south, which can be seen as the unknown, the mysterious, or the spiritual.
The fact that they are frightened and scared can be seen as a normal reaction to entering the unknown

In another version, the boy is left in a canoe at the chief's village, and the chief and his people do not know what to do with the boy, and they ask the boy's father what they should do with the boy, and his father tells them to let the boy starve, because he is an unwanted boy.

This story is told in the Tlingit language by a native Tlingit storyteller. It is a story about two young hunters who go down to the river to hunt seals. They are young and inexperienced and are afraid of the big, dark night. They hear a bear roaring in the distance and they run away. They make their way back to the village and they are safe.
The story is a simple one, told in a straightforward manner. The two young hunters are the protagonists and they are the ones who are afraid of the night and the unknown. The sound of a bear roaring in the distance is a common fear for hunters in the wilderness, and the story makes use of this fear to move the plot along. The climax of the story is when the two young hunters are running back to the village, away from the unknown sounds in the darkness. The resolution of the story comes when they reach the safety of the village, and the story ends there.
The story is a classic example of a "coming home" story, a story where the protagonists are young and inexperienced and must learn to survive in the wilderness. They saw a huge ball of fire coming toward them. It came nearer and nearer, and they could feel its heat. Then it burst into a thousand pieces and was gone. They called the place where they saw the fireballs "The Place of the Falling Stars," and that is what we call it today.

They ran for their canoe and were just able to push it out onto the river before the Wendigo landed on the shore.  It was a large, hump-backed creature with sharp teeth and glowing eyes.  They tried to paddle away but the Wendigo reached down and capsized their canoe.  It turned the men over and ate one of them.  Then it took the other man up onto its back and carried him away.

The next day a group of men went in search of the missing man.  They found the first man's body and followed the tracks of the Wendigo until dark.  Then they heard the Wendigo calling and they ran away.  The next day they followed the tracks again and came upon the Wendigo as it was eating the second man.  They attacked it with their guns and clubs and were able to drive it away.  They found the rest of the man's body later.

The Wendigo was not seen again for many years.  Then, in the winter of 1897, it appeared again and caused great damage in Egulac.  It would come out only when the temperature went below zero.  It would creep into the houses at night and eat the people while they were sleeping.  A group of men went after it and were able to drive it away.  They set traps and managed to capture one of its feet.  They cut off the foot and took it back to the village to prove that they had killed the Wendigo.

But the Wendigo was not dead.  It was still out there in the woods, waiting to come back and kill again.

The two young men went to the sound of the voices and found a group of people standing there, all dressed in furs with their heads covered. The brothers tried to talk to them but no one would answer them. The people were all from different tribes and had been exiled from their own tribes for various reasons. They had sought refuge with the tribe that had exiled them but their own kinsmen would not take them back. They had been wandering for many months and were lost.
One of the young men, in his pity for these poor outcasts, said to them, "My brothers, what is the matter? Why do you stand here all covered up and not answer us? We are your brothers and we will help you."
The people were startled and amazed that anyone would take any interest in them. They told the young men their sad stories and begged for their help. The two young men agreed to take the group to their own tribe and ask for their forgiveness.
The group of people followed the two young men to their tribe. The tribe was astonished to see them returning with this group of people. The brothers explained to their tribe the sad stories of these people and begged for their forgiveness for these their brothers. The tribe was touched by their brothers' love for these outcasts and forgave them all. The people who had been exiled were overjoyed and grateful.
The two young men had brought about a reunion of brothers who had been separated for many months and even years. They had also taught their tribe a great lesson of love and forgiveness.

While they were there, a great flood came and the water rose over the land and destroyed everything. The two young men climbed onto the top of a tall tree to escape the water, and they sat there while everything around them was destroyed. When the flood had gone down, they climbed down from the tree and found that everything was covered in mud. Everything was different, and they could not find their way home. They met another young man, and they asked him to take them to his village, and he took them to his village and gave them food to eat and things to wear. They lived with him and his family for a while, but they wanted to find their own village, so they set out to look for it. They traveled for a long time, and one day they saw a woman in the distance. They went to her and asked her if she knew where Egulac was. She told them that she was from Egulac, but that it was different now. She took them to her house, and she and her family gave them food to eat and things to wear. She told them that they could stay there for the winter, but in the spring they should go back to their own village. In the spring they set out to look for their village again. They followed the sun and found their village, but it was different. Everything had been rebuilt in a different place, and everything was different. They went to a chief's house and asked the chief if he knew where their village had been. The chief told them that he was the chief of the village now, and that their village had been destroyed in a flood, and everyone had to start over. Everything had to be rebuilt in a different place. The young men were upset, but they stayed in the village and lived there for the rest of their lives.

The flood is interpreted as a metaphor for the effects of colonialism on indigenous peoples' lives; the two young men's inability to find their way home despite the help of a native guide represents the difficulties the Natives faced in adapting to the new world order.

Background
In the myths of many Native American tribes, Coyote is a trickster figure who often appears in stories as a shape-shifter. This story is from the Kwakiutl people of the Pacific Northwest. They are part of the larger group of people known as the First Nations.
The Kwakiutl have a matrilineal society, meaning that female lines of descent and family relationships are important in their culture. The Kwakiutl are also known for their elaborate potlatch ceremonies.

The story
Nakon was out hunting seals with his brother when it became foggy and calm. They heard a sound like a man running and leaping over the water. Then they saw a light over the water and a man with a bow and arrow racing toward them. Nakon and his brother were both hit by arrows, which sank into their shoulders. Nakon told them that he was the son of Nootka and that he was trying to kill a great white whale that lived at the end of the world. He said that he had shot the two young men because he was in a hurry.
Nakon and his brother helped Nakon for three days. Nakon told them that the arrow in his shoulder was his mother's arrow and that he had to return it to her. He told them that he would be back the next year to continue his hunt.
The next year, Nakon came back with his family. The two young men helped Nakon and his family for three days. Then Nakon left to continue his hunt.

Then they heard voices and words flying about as they could not see in the fog. The voices seemed to be coming from two canoes which were arguing over a woman. The two young men listened and then realized that the voices were those of Hila and Hilbeto, two spirits who were in love with each other. The two spirits were arguing over a young woman who had jilted Hila and was now in Hilbeto's canoe. The young woman wanted to go to her family, but Hilbeto wanted to take her away with him. Hila said she should go to her family, but he wanted her for himself. The two spirits argued for a long time, and then they heard the voices of the two young men and knew that they were there listening. 
They called out to the young men and invited them into the canoes.  Then the spirits took the two young men to their village, where they were welcomed and given gifts of fish and furs.  The spirits told them many stories and taught them many things.  Then the spirits took the two young men to the place where the sun rises and there they changed them into swans and they became spirit swans.  The spirits told them that they could stay with them as long as they wanted and that they would become spirits when they died.  Then the spirits took them back to their own village and there they lived happily ever after.

They heard a sound like the hum of a swarm of bees and it seemed to come from the water. They couldn't see the source of the sound but they saw a light over the water which seemed to be moving up and down. They called the sound "the hum of the water spirits". They heard the sound again the next night and went to investigate. They found a canoe beached near the village, and in the canoe they saw a man whose skin was like a white fur. The man was rowing toward them but when he saw the two young men he went back to the village. The two young men followed him to the village and hid behind some bushes. The man went into a house and they could see him changing his clothes. He came out wearing a shirt and trousers like white fur. He went down to the beach and called out "Soon I will be able to wear red fur." The two young men went home and told their people about the man they had seen. The people said that the man must have been Tleetustle, the Water Spirit.

Suddenly a great wave arose and rushed inland with a roaring noise. It carried away everything before it. When it reached the two young men it swept them away and carried them out to sea. The next morning the people went to the place where the young men had been hunting and saw that a great wave had come in and covered the beach with sand. They looked for the young men but could not find them.

An old man remembered that once long ago a similar thing had happened and two men had been taken out to sea. He suggested that the same thing had happened again and that the young men were dead. The people went out in canoes to look for the young men. After searching all day they found them on a small island not far from the mainland. They were cold and hungry, but otherwise well. The people brought them home and were very glad to see that they were safe.

The old man said to the people, "This is the second time that this has happened. I think that the two young men are being kept here for some reason. Perhaps they were chosen to be taken out to sea so that they could tell people about the time when the water came in and covered the beach. I think that they were chosen to tell people about this because they are the only two people who can remember it."

The people were very happy that the two young men had been saved. They were happy because they thought that the young men would be able to tell them about the time when the water came in and covered the beach.

Suddenly a great wave arose and in an instant the men were enveloped in darkness. The sky was hidden from view and when the fog lifted the sun was shining again. They searched for their canoe but it was nowhere to be found. They called out to each other in the darkness and their voices echoed back to them from the hills. They were lost. They called out once more and heard their voices cry out in the distance. Then they were silent. They had called out to each other and their voices had carried the message across the water to their village and the people came and rescued them.

One day a canoe with two young men went down the river to fish. They had gone a short distance when they heard a cry for help. They rowed towards the cry and saw a man on a large rock in the middle of the river. They asked him what had happened. The man said that he had been fishing by himself and his canoe had capsized and he was unable to turn it right side up. The two young men tried to help him but it was of no use. They could not turn the canoe right side up. They tried to get the man into their canoe but he was too heavy for them. They tried to swim to the rock but the man was too heavy for them to lift onto the rock. They swam back to their canoe and tried to turn it over again but it would not budge. They were tired now and were not able to help the man. They rested for a while and then tried again. This time they were able to turn the canoe over and placed the man in it. They rowed to the man's canoe and righted it. Then they all returned to the village together.

One day a man was out in his canoe fishing by himself. He had caught several fish and was content. He was just about to turn back towards the village when he heard a cry for help. He looked around and saw a man waving his arms for help. The man in the canoe tried to help the other man to his canoe but the man in the water was too far away and the canoe was too heavy to lift into the water. The man tried to swim to the other man but he was tired and could not make it. He called out to the man to come to him but the man in the water could not hear him.

Then they heard a sound like the sound of a large bell or like the sound of a waterfall.  They paddled toward the sound and saw a great light bearing down on them.  When it came close they saw that it was a herd of caribou with antlers glistening in the moonlight.  The caribou were being chased by a large bear.
The two young men took up their paddles and shot at the bear, but it did not stop.  It was huge and its mouth was huge too and it had great big teeth.  One of the young men was afraid and he made the sign of fear and the bear roared and stopped roaring only when it was out of breath.  Then it charged at them again.
The two young men were very afraid and they paddled as fast as they could toward the herd of caribou.  The bear was chasing them and it was roaring and making a terrible noise.  The herd of caribou were also making a noise like bells ringing.  The bear was almost upon them when the herd of caribou opened up into a great herd of caribou and the bear was gone.  The young men were very glad.
They went back to Egulac and told what had happened to them.  They said that it was the largest bear they had ever seen and that it had a large mouth and great big teeth and that it roared terribly.  They said that they had paddled as fast as they could toward the herd of caribou and that the herd had opened up into a large herd just as they were getting to it, and that the bear had gone away.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the sound of a big bell, and then another and still another. The sound came from the water and it was so loud that it woke up the whole village. The young men were afraid and they ran back to the village. They told everyone they met along the way what had happened and soon everyone was running to the river to see what had happened. When they got there they saw that the bell-like sounds were coming from the waters of the river. The sounds were so loud that they could be heard for miles. They were coming from the steles that had been put in the river by the Chinese explorers. The Chinese had filled the steles with gunpowder and when the fog was so thick that everything was covered up, they fired their guns into the air to let the natives know that they were there. This was the signal that the Chinese used to tell the natives that they were coming. The natives called the bell-like sound "the Chinese calling their gods."

They saw a great light in the sky and it was coming toward them. They thought it was a large sailing ship and were pleased, as they wanted to go home. The light came closer and closer and they could see it was not a ship but a big ball of fire. They were afraid and hid under some bushes. They were not hurt, but they were afraid to look out again. Then they heard a voice calling them. They were afraid, but they called back, "We are here, we are human beings." The voice told them to come out and they did. The ball of fire was a UFO. Inside were six little men, dressed in silver suits. They were surprised to see the men and wanted to know who they were and where they came from. The young men told them, and the little men said they came from Mars. They had been watching the earth for a long time and had never seen anyone throw a spear before. They wanted to learn how it was done. They showed the young men some things from their planet and then they went back into their ship. They took the two young men to Mars to show them their world. It was a beautiful place with rivers and lakes and oceans. It was different from the earth but nice. They were there for a long time and learned many things. Then the little men took them back to their own time and place. They were glad to be back, but they were happy they had seen Mars.

Analysis
The story begins with an event that is common in many UFO narratives: two men are out late at night, in a secluded place, when a UFO appears. The description of the UFO as a "ball of fire" is also common in UFO reports, dating back to at least the 1940s. The description of the aliens as little men in silver suits is reminiscent of the "grays" of popular culture. The aliens' claim that they have been watching Earth for a long time and have never seen a spear thrown before is a common theme in abduction narratives. The aliens' home planet, Mars, is a common origin for extraterrestrial beings in popular culture. The story ends with the aliens taking the two young men to Mars and showing them its beauty, suggesting a positive view of the aliens' motives.

The two men sat down at the edge of the river to rest and they saw a light across the river. They went closer to the light and saw that it was a canoe full of people. The people in the canoe were singing and dancing and having a good time. The two young men wanted to join in and they asked the people in the canoe where they were from. The people in the canoe said that they were from a land far away.
The two young men asked if they could go to this land and they said yes. So the two young men went with them and they had a good time. But after a while they wanted to go home and they asked the people in the canoe to take them back. The people in the canoe said no and they refused to take them back. So the two young men had to swim back by themselves.
When they got back to their camp they saw that their canoe was gone. They went down to the river to look for it and they saw the people from the other canoe coming towards them. The people in the canoe said that they had taken the two young men's canoe by mistake. They said that they were from a land far away and they didn't mean to take the canoe. They offered to take the two young men with them again and the two young men said yes.
So the four people got into the canoe and they went to the land where the people were singing and dancing. And there they had a good time. And after a while they went back to their own land.
This story is told by a Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) storyteller and it is a story about how stories spread from place to place. It is also a story about how people should be respectful and kind to each other.

Notes
This story is from the Tsimshian people, collected and transcribed by Franz Boas in 1885. It is one of the few myths from the Tsimshian to survive the 20th Century. It is also one of the few myths from the Tsimshian to be published in English translation.
It is one of the most popular of Tsimshian myths and is often told to tourists.
The Taku River flows into the Pacific Ocean just north of Prince Rupert.
The Tsimshian have a matrilineal society, so the phrase "women and children" does not imply that only women and children were present, but rather that the men were not present.

The story of the Daughters of Old Man and the Sons of Old Man Woman is a creation myth of the Nuu-chah-nulth people of the west coast of Vancouver Island. It was written down by James Alexander Teit, a ethnologist for the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia, from the storytelling of John Henry (Ka'yu'p'i'yu') of the Ah-tah-choo band of the Tseshaht people in 1909.

The young men reached Egulac safely and told what had happened. The people then decided to move to a place of safety across the river. Everything was carried to the canoes and then they were pushed off so that the people could paddle safely across the river.
Just before they left Egulac a great wave came from the mountain and roared down the river. This wave carried away everything that had been left behind, even the poles and canoes that had been used to cross the river.

Then they knew that they would live for ever in a world of happiness and joy.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roar of a thousand cannons. It was the sound of a thousand cannons because it was the sound of a thousand canoes. It was the sound of the Egulac canoes coming home from the war.
The young men ran to the shore to meet their canoes and their relatives who were returning from war. The canoes were filled with wounded. The young men helped their relatives out of the canoes and onto the shore. Their relatives were not like the young men any longer. They had changed. They had become like giants. They were tall and strong and their skin was no longer like the skin of young men. It was like the bark of trees. The young men had never seen their relatives like this before. They had become great men. They had become great hunters.
The young men helped their relatives inland to their lodges. There they were washed and their wounds were dressed. The young men fed their relatives and then they listened while their relatives told them about the war.
The first one told about how he had been out in the canoe with his paddle in his hand when an enemy canoe came up alongside him. He had tried to strike his enemy down but his enemy was too strong. He had fought and fought until he had pushed his enemy overboard. He had swum to where his enemy was swimming and he had grabbed him by the hair and pushed his head under the water until he drowned.
The second one told how he had been in the rear of the battle. He had been fighting hand to hand with his enemy when he had seen a large boulder coming towards him. It was his enemy. His enemy had picked up a boulder and was coming towards him with it in his hand. The young man had grabbed his enemy's wrist and had twisted it until he had dropped the boulder. Then he had taken his enemy by the hair and had thrown him down. He had struck him over and over again until he was dead.
The third one told how he had been surrounded by many enemies. He had fought them all off but he was wounded. He had been wounded by a spear that had gone in under his arm and out over his back. He had rolled over and over until the spear came out. He had picked up a large stick and had clubbed his enemies until they were all dead.

The young man was not afraid any longer and went to the spirit and received a bundle of sweet grass.

The spirit then spoke to the other young man and said: "What makes you run away? I am your relative. Come to me and I will give you a good gift." The young man was afraid and would not come. The spirit then spoke to him in a loud voice and said: "I will not speak to you again. I will only roar to you. Come to me or I will take you away." The young man was very afraid and ran to the spirit and received a bundle of sweet grass.
Then the two young men went home and told the old people what had happened. The old people were glad and said: "The spirit of the river is our relative. We must always treat it with respect. We must not take more than we need from it. We must leave some for the next person and for the spirit."
And the old people said: "We will make a good gift for the spirit of the river. We will make it a canoe filled with sweet grass."
So they made a canoe and filled it with sweet grass and left it by the river. And the spirit was pleased and helped them from then on.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roaring of a mighty waterfall. They listened and then heard it again. They followed the sound and found themselves at the foot of a huge waterfall.
They were awed by its beauty and power. As they stood there, a mighty voice called out, "This is the Fall of the River of Time. Many a man has stood at this place and marvelled at its beauty. Many a man has passed from this world at this place."
The two young men were afraid and turned to leave. As they reached the edge of the river they heard the voice again, "Take courage, young men. Do not be afraid. Go back to your camp and tell your people that I, Gichi Manidoo, the Great Spirit, have spoken to you. Tell them that I say that the time is near when I will gather all of the people of this world to me, and a great flood will cover the earth and all that is upon it. And I will make a new world, a world of beauty and peace. And there will be no more sickness or suffering.
The two young men returned to their camp and told their people what had happened. The people were amazed and many were afraid. They asked many questions and the two young men told them everything that had happened.
Then the people of Egulac went to the place of the waterfall and they saw that it was true. They knew that the Great Spirit was mighty and powerful and that he would keep his word. And so they lived their lives in peace and happiness, knowing that the Great Spirit would keep his word and make a new world.
And it was so. The Great Spirit gathered all of the people of the world to him and a great flood covered the earth and all that was upon it. And there was a new world of beauty and peace and there was no more sickness or suffering. And the people of Egulac were happy and content.

The Haida people lived in the area now known as Taku Inlet in northern British Columbia for thousands of years before European contact. The Haida people were a self-sufficient society who hunted, fished, and gathered food from the land. The Haida people were known for their skill in carving and for their beautiful wooden canoes.
The Haida people had a rich mythological tradition. They believed that the world was created in seven days, just like in the Christian story of creation. As they approached the edge of the cliff they saw that the source of the sound was a mighty waterfall falling over a cliff into the sea. They stood there and marveled at the beauty of it and then they noticed that the waterfall was not falling from the cliff but was pushed over by a great force. They decided to investigate that force and found that it was the wind. They were amazed and wondered how it was possible for wind to be so powerful. They stood there and marveled at the power of the wind as it pushed the waterfall over the cliff. They then returned to their camp and related to their tribe members what they had seen and learned.

Interpretation
The story is an example of an informative myth. It describes and explains a natural phenomenon. In this case, the myth explains the creation of a waterfall due to wind. It shows that the wind has great power, and that it can create something as beautiful as a waterfall.

Comparisons
This story is similar to the Greek myth of Orion and the Giant's Daughter, in which a young man discovers the power of the wind. It is also similar to the Japanese myth of the birth of the wind gods, in which the wind gods are born from the tears of the god of the sea.

Her father said "You must give a potlatch to prove that you are worthy to marry my daughter." Nootka went home to Egulac and held a potlatch. He invited everyone in the village and in Tlowit'ses. He gave away everything that he had. He gave away canoes, copper, blankets, and fish. He gave away everything that he had. Then he asked for the hand of the young woman. She consented and they were married.
After the wedding, the young couple went to Egulac to live. Nootka's father was very happy and he invited everyone in Egulac and Tlowit'ses to a feast. Nootka and his wife served the people. After the feast, there was a dance. Nootka and his wife danced and everyone danced. They danced until the sun came up. Then everyone went home. Nootka and his wife went to his house and they went to bed.
In the morning, the sun came up and the people went home. Nootka and his wife lived happily ever after. They had many children and their children had children. They all lived happily ever after.

The story is told by Maude B. Brown, a Kwakiutl Native American, in her book "Myths and Legends of the Kwakiutl Indians" (1930).

Captain John Davis was on his way to England after a long voyage when his ship was caught in a storm. The storm drove his ship up the St. Lawrence River and he was unable to sail back down again because the river was closed by ice. He was forced to winter in the country of the Iroquois. He lived with them for a year and learned their language and their ways. In the spring he built a canoe and started on his journey home. He had been sailing for many days when his ship was driven ashore in a storm on the coast of New York. He walked for many days through the woods and finally came to the village of the Mohawks. While he was there he learned that a party of English traders was to pass through the village on their way to trade with the tribes in the interior. He went with them and was soon among his own people in Albany.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roar of a bear, then another, and yet another, and then all hell broke loose. The two young men ran for their canoe and started to push their way out to sea. They had not gone far when they heard a loud splash and a wave came over their canoe, and then another and another, until they were swamped and drowned.
For a long time the two young men from Egulac lay at the bottom of the river bed, trapped in their canoe. Then the current changed and they slowly began to travel down the river toward the sea.
As they neared the end of the river they could hear the roar of the sea lions and the crashing of the waves. Soon they were in the sea and the two young men swam to a small island not far from the shore. There they found a cave and crawled in to wait the next tide.
The next tide came in and they were able to swim to the mainland, but as they walked along the beach they saw a bear standing on its hind legs and they ran inland to hide. The bear roared and they thought it was going to throw a boulder on them, but instead it picked up a salmon and ate it. After a while the two young men from Egulac worked their way back to their village.
They told the people what had happened to them and everyone was amazed at their good luck. From then on the two young men never went down to the river to hunt seals at night, but they would often tell the story of how they were swallowed by the river and how they were saved by the tide.

The story of the Two Young Men from Egulac is a traditional Arikara myth.

While they were there, a great flood came and swept them away. And the young men were not able to get back to Egulac.
The next morning a young woman came down to the river to wash her clothing. When she reached the river she saw the footprints of a man and a woman.  Following the footprints she saw a canoe which had been covered with dirt and grass.  She washed the canoe and made it clean and then she saw the two young men sitting in the canoe looking very cold and hungry.  They told her that they had been swept away by the flood and had been lost for a very long time.  They were very happy to be back in Egulac.
The young woman told the young men that she was very glad that she had found them and that she would never let them starve or be lost again.  She would always take care of them from that day on.
The young men never forgot the kind young woman who had found them and taken care of them.  They lived with her in Egulac and they were always very happy.

The story of the two young men and the flood is a story that has been told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people of the west coast of Vancouver Island for a very long time.  It is a story about the importance of being kind and taking care of each other.  It is also a story about the power of nature and the dangers of being overconfident.  The story has many variations, but the basic plot remains the same.
The story has been passed down through oral tradition for centuries.  It is part of the Nuu-chah-nulth creation story, which explains how the world was created and how people first came to live on the west coast of Vancouver Island.

Then they heard voices and sounds all around them. At first, they thought it was a large party of people but soon realized that the sounds were coming from the spirits of the dead. The two young men were terrified and begged for the spirits to let them go. The spirits refused and then began to predict the future. They said that a great storm was coming and that it would destroy Egulac. They said that after the storm there would be five years of famine and then a new leader would arise and bring great wealth to Egulac. The two young men were so terrified that they ran back to Egulac and told everyone about the spirits' prediction.

The people of Egulac did not believe them and the young men were scorned and laughed at. However, as the days passed, the weather became warmer and sunnier than ever before and everyone was happy. Then, one day, a huge storm came and destroyed Egulac. It was exactly as the spirits had predicted. The people of Egulac were all killed or hurt and the village was destroyed. Five years later, a new leader did arise and he did bring great wealth to Egulac. The people of Egulac never forgot the two young men and the spirits' prediction.

This story is similar to the European folk tale "The Legend of the Bianco D'Aqua".

When she came back she called out to the young men and beckoned to them to come. They went to her and she took one of them and put him in the canoe and took the other and put him in the canoe also. They rowed for a long time and then she stopped at a place where there was a house. She took the two young men inside and they saw that she was a young woman after all. She cooked some food and they ate it. Then she took the two young men to her bed and they were her lovers until morning. Suddenly a large wave picked them up and carried them a long way up the river. It set them down at the place where the man named Hailah was sleeping. Hailah was a young man of great power and he had been sleeping for four days. When the two young men woke him up they told him what had happened. Hailah told them to go back to the place where they had been picked up and he went with them. When they got there they saw a great light in the sky and a voice came from the light. The voice said: "The son of a man of power has been conceived. He will be born in four days. In three days the sun will rise in the west and set in the east. In two days the people will not be able to breathe. When these things happen, the son of a man of power will be conceived." Then the light went out and the sun came up.

Analysis
The story is about a prophecy that predicts the birth of a man of power. The prophecy includes a solar myth in which the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, and a lunar myth in which people cannot breathe for two days. These myths may represent the Zuni Seventh Day and Ninth Day prophecies. The story may also represent the creation of the sun and moon. The Zuni believe that the sun and moon arose from the same place at the same time. The sun is male and the moon is female. They are children of the Earth-Maker.

Suddenly a great light appeared over the river and many people came down to the river to see it. The light moved towards them and there in the water appeared a great canoe made out of white stone, and in the canoe were many white people, all naked.
There were chiefs and warriors and they were all naked. They had long hair and beards and their skin was white. They sat in their canoe as still as statues and they did not move.
The Egulac men were afraid and they crouched down behind a log and did not move or make a sound. They were afraid of the white people.
Then one of the white people stood up in the canoe and spoke to the people on the shore. He said: "We are the people who have come from across the water. We have come to take possession of this land. We have come to take the fur-bearing animals and all the game from this land, and we will make the people here our slaves. We will make slaves of you and your wives and your children. We will make slaves of all the people here and we will drive you before us like dogs."
Then the great light went out and the white people in the canoe disappeared and the canoe disappeared and the people of Egulac came out from behind the log and ran to their canoes and paddled to their homes.

They heard voices and then saw two lights coming towards them. They were not afraid because they knew the spirits were good and meant them no harm. The spirits introduced themselves as the Thunderers. They invited the two young men to come with them to their village. The men refused and the spirits offered to give them anything they wanted. The men asked for two things: that their nets would be full of fish and that they would be protected from the Thunderers when they were hunting seals. The spirits agreed and then disappeared.

The next morning the two young men went out to their nets and they were full of fish. They were very happy and told their elders about the spirits. Their elders said that this was a good thing because the Thunderers are good spirits.  The young men went out to hunt seals and they saw a big seal bear. One of the spirits spoke to them and said, "We are going to take you to our village." They went and the spirits gave them their choice of anything they wanted. They chose to have their nets full of fish and to be protected from the Thunderers when they were hunting seals. The spirits agreed and then took them to their village. It was a beautiful place with many houses and many people. The spirits told them that they could stay for a while and then they would take them back to their own village.
The young men stayed for a while and then the spirits took them back to their own village. They were very happy and thanked the spirits. From then on their nets were always full of fish and they were always protected when they were hunting seals. They told their story everywhere they went and everyone was happy for them.

The ship's captain tries to turn the ship around but it capsizes, throwing all the crew members into the water. The two young men swim to the ship and climb aboard. They find that everyone has survived the capsizing, but they can't get the fire out.
One of the sailors suggests that they try to get to the shore, but the other says that it's too far and that they should try to put the fire out again. As they are debating what to do, the ship suddenly explodes, killing everyone on board.
The two young men swim back to the shore and tell everyone what happened. The next day, a group of people goes to the site of the shipwreck to salvage what they can. As they are working, they hear a strange noise. Suddenly, the ship's smokestack falls out of the sky and lands on the group, killing everyone except for one man. The man looks up and sees that a cloud is forming the shape of the ship's name, "Vancouver".

The girl told this story to her family and they went to the river to find out what had happened to the two young men.  They found out that a large wave had come and covered everything in its path.  The two men were swept away and their bodies were never found.

The two spirits stayed at the river and watched over each other.  They became trapped in the sand at the bottom of the river.  They could not leave until they found out what had happened to them.  They could see everything that went on around them but they could not leave.

Sometimes when the tide goes out, you can see the spirits of the two young men standing on the banks of the river.  They are still watching over the river and they are still trying to find out what happened to them.  They are still there today, over 1000 years later.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the hum of a swarm of bees, and then they saw a great light in the sky. They were afraid to look at it and they crouched down and hid their faces. Then everything became still again, and they saw that the light was coming from a large, long, flat object that was hovering over the water. They could see seven poles or legs extending from the sides of this thing, and they could see people or shapes moving up and down the sides of the legs. The young men were afraid, and they ran away to hide. They were not sure what they had seen, but they thought it was a bad dream.

The story is told from the perspective of an unnamed narrator who heard the story from an old man. The old man was not there when the event took place, but he was told the story by a man who was there and who saw it all. The event took place "a long time ago," and the old man had lived a very long life, so it is difficult to place a date on the event. It is possible that the event took place in the 18th century, but it could have taken place at any time in the previous two hundred years. The location is also not clear, as the old man said the event took place "up the coast a little way," and he was referring to a place where there were many Egulac people. The two young men who had the experience were not named, and no other details were given about them.

Interpretation
The story has been interpreted as a description of a UFO sighting, and it has also been interpreted as a description of a Thunderbird. However, the old man who told the story said that he thought the two young men were having a bad dream, and he thought the story was a bad dream. He did not think it really happened.

They saw a light in the distance, and thinking it was a fisherman's lantern, they rowed toward it. As they got closer, they realized that the light was not from a lantern but from a canoe, and in the canoe was a woman. The woman was singing a song, and as they listened they heard that it was a love song directed to them. They were so entranced by her song that they went closer still, and when they reached her, they found she had no face. In some versions, they are captivated and try to row toward her, but in other versions they are repulsed and try to row away. She stopped singing and told them that she was a spirit of the water and that she had heard their song and was moved by it. She offered to give them a gift. The first asked for gold and jewels, but she gave him nothing. The second asked for a song that would help him through the world, and she gave him a song that would enable him to win the love of any woman he met. Then she pushed them away from her canoe and disappeared.

Analysis
This myth has a number of similarities with the legend of the Maid of Misery. Both feature a spirit of the water who falls in love with two men at once, and who offers each of them a gift. The first is offered material wealth and rejects it, and the second is offered a song that will help him win the love of women. There are a number of differences, however. In this myth, it is the two men who go to the water to hunt seals, and they are drawn to the spirit by her singing. In the legend of the Maid of Misery, it is the Maid who goes to the men's camp and offers to marry the man who can answer her riddle. In this myth, it is the men who are transfixed by the sight of the spirit and by her singing, and they are only able to move once she has spoken to them. In the legend of the Maid of Misery, the men are able to see her when they wake up the next morning. In this myth, the men are not able to see her face.

In the summer of 1878, two young men from the village of Egulac in British Columbia went down to the river to hunt seals. The river was very calm and the sky was overcast. The two young men were out in a canoe on the river, and they were using torches to light their way. They had been out on the river for a while and they had caught a few seals, when suddenly the sky grew dark and a thick fog came down over the river. The two young men were unable to see where they were going and they became disoriented. They tried to paddle back to the shore but the current was strong and it carried them out into the middle of the river. Suddenly, without warning, a great wave rose up out of the fog and swallowed the canoe and the two young men who were in it. The wave was like a wall of water that rose up higher than the trees along the riverbank. It was higher than the hills along the riverbank. It was higher than the mountains along the riverbank. It was higher than the clouds in the sky. And it was wider than the sky. And it was still rising.

The two young men were gone in an instant. They were swallowed up by the great wave and they were never seen or heard of again.

The people of Egulac were very sad when they learned that their two young men had disappeared. They searched for them along the riverbank and they searched up and down the river but they were never able to find any trace of them. They searched for days and days but they were never found.

Context
This story is from the Kwakiutl people of the northwest coast of North America. It is a version of a creation story. The story is told by a man who has been watching a ceremonial dance. He is asked what he thinks the dancers are dancing about and he says that he doesn't know. The story is told as a way to explain how the people came to live on the island.

Analysis
This story is a legend about how the people of Egulac came to live on an island. The story was written down by Franz Boas in 1897. Boas was a German-born, Canadian-American anthropologist who is considered to be the father of American anthropology. The story is told in the form of a narrative.
The story is about two young men who go down to the river to hunt seals. They get caught in a fog and a large wave comes and takes them out to sea. They end up on a piece of debris that is floating in the water. They stay there until the sun rises and then they see that it is an island. They live there for some time and then they go back to Egulac in a canoe.
The story is a creation myth. It explains how the people of Egulac came to live on an island. The story also shows the importance of the sea and the river to the Kwakiutl people. The story also shows the importance of hunting seals. The story also shows that even though the two young men were lost and stranded they were able to survive and make it back to Egulac.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roar of a thousand thunderclaps. They looked around and saw a large column of water rising up and then sink back into the river. They thought that it must have been a whale spouting water as it dived, but they did not know it was a volcano erupting. 
The young men had been hunting seals near the mouth of the Columbia River in what is now Oregon. They were members of the Chinook tribe, and it was around 1783 AD.
The volcano that erupted was Mount St. Helens. The eruption was the first in a series of four major eruptions at the mountain. The largest took place in 1806, and the last occurred in 1857. 
The young men continued to hear rumbling sounds and see columns of water rising up and then sink back into the river for the rest of the night. When they went back to the river the next day, they saw that the shoreline had changed, with new sandbars having formed. They went back to their village and told everyone about the thunderclaps, the shaking ground, and the new sandbars.
The story was told and retold, and it became part of the oral history of the Chinook tribe. It was passed down from one generation to the next, until it was recorded by ethnologist Franz Boas in the late 1800s.

The young men went back to their village and told everyone about the spirits and about the old woman's request. Her spirit was there though and she was pleased with the sealskins and gave the young men their golden weapons.

Then the man swept the floor one last time, turned around and disappeared into the forest. The two young men stood there and looked after him. Then they went home. The next day they told their elders what had happened. Their elders said, "That was the Wind Man. He comes out when the weather is calm and foggy in the winter nights. He makes that sound and sweeps the floor in front of him. He does this three times. Then he goes home to the south. He is the wind that blows in the winter nights."


== Notes ==

They saw a light in the sky which was a UFO. They landed and found that there were three men inside, who were from Jupiter. They had a strange language but the young men understood them. The Jupiter men were looking for a place to land when they saw the smoke of the young men's campfire. They were friendly and showed the young men their pictures of their home planet. They also showed them how to make a stone fly. They left after a while, leaving the young men with a strange feeling.

Analysis
The story is likely a traditional story that has been influenced by contact with Western UFO culture. The similarity of the Jupiter men's home planet to our own is likely a coincidence, and the story may have originally involved a different planet or celestial body that was altered to fit in the new cultural context. The story may also be a dream narrative.

The word "seals" in the story is "pikuni," which means "seals" in the Blackfoot language.  The word "egulac" means "fog" in the Blackfoot language.

Discussion
The story is a warning about going out on the water when it is foggy.  The two young men in the story went out to hunt seals at night, which is not allowed.  The word "pikuni" in the story is a Blackfoot word that means "seals."  Seals were an important food source for the Blackfoot people.  The Blackfoot people hunted seals using nets and clubs.  They would hide in canoes while the seals were resting on land and then rush out and club them.  The Blackfoot people also used dog teams to go after the seals.  The dogs would chase the seals onto the ice and the Blackfoot people would throw spears at the seals.  The word "egulac" in the story means "fog."  Fog is a common occurrence on the Great Plains and in the Rocky Mountains.  The story is a warning about going out on the water when it is foggy.  The two young men in the story went out in the middle of the night when it was foggy.  They were swept out to the middle of the river and were lost.  The story warns that this can happen to anyone who goes out on the water when it is foggy.  The story also warns against going out at night to hunt seals because it is dangerous.  The story is a reminder that nature can be dangerous and unpredictable and that people should be careful and respectful of nature.  The story also shows that sometimes people can make mistakes and pay the price for those mistakes.

The young men did not answer. Then the mermaid called out, "I know where you are going. I know where you are going." The young men were afraid and they ran away. They went to their canoes and they paddled away as fast as they could.

The mermaids were not angry with them. They continued to have their party on the water. But from then on every time two young men went down to the river to hunt seals the mermaids would come out of the water and call for Te-kah-min and Te-kah-min-ah. And every time the young men would run away afraid.

This story is told by the Nisqually people.  Te-kah-min means "seal" and Te-kah-min-ah means "seal woman" or "mermaid".

Analysis
This story is similar to other canoe stories such as that of Huya and Ulkas, and that of the Dena'ina people.  It is also similar to the story of the canoe in "The Adventures of Hudo and His Companions" in which two young men are taken in by a foreign group of people after a natural disaster.  Both of these stories feature natural disasters and the formation of relationships between groups of people.  The fact that the two young men in this story become brothers to the Haida people shows the close relationship that the Haida people share with everyone.  This story also shows that despite the differences between groups of people, they can form close relationships.

This story is about death. The two young men go on a journey into the spirit world, where they are welcomed and given gifts. This story is similar to the legend of Cain and Abel, and to the story of Noah's Ark in the Bible.  It is also similar to the stories of the Sumerian King List, where a king builds an ark and survives a flood that was sent by the gods to destroy the human race because of their wickedness.  The story is also similar to the Chinese legend of the Yellow Emperor.
There are many versions of this story.  This version was told to anthropologist James Teit by a Native American informant in the Okanagan Valley of British Columbia.

Analysis
This story may be a creation myth, as it explains how the people came to be where they are now.  It also explains how their ancestors survived a catastrophic flood.  The story also seems to be a flood myth, as it describes the destruction of a village by a flood.  The story may also be a hero myth, as it describes how two young men survived the flood and then searched for their people.  The story may also be a coming of age myth, as it describes how the two young men had to learn to survive in a new world.

While they were there they heard voices and they went to investigate. They saw a canoe approaching them and the canoe was filled with people. These people were spirits, and they invited the two young men to come and live with them. The two young men refused and they went back to their camp.

The two men were suddenly seized by a great fear and began to run. They had not run far when they heard the roar of a large water monster. They were soon overtaken by the monster, and just as it was about to swallow them whole, they jumped into the water and swam to the shore. The monster then turned its attention to the other man and swallowed him whole.

The young man who had escaped ran back to his village and told his story. The people of the village didn't believe him, and some even accused him of causing the death of his friend by sorcery.

The next day, the father of the man who had been swallowed by the monster went down to the river to search for his son. He had not gone far when he too was seized by a great fear and began to run. He ran until he reached the spot where his son had been swallowed. He begged the monster to give him back his son and promised to give the monster a potlatch in return. The monster agreed to this and spat the young man out. His father was overjoyed to see his son alive, and they both ran back to the village.

When they arrived, the people of the village would not believe them, and once again, the young man was accused of causing his own death by sorcery.  The two men then decided to go to the village of the white people (Europeans) to prove that they were not sorcerers. They traveled by canoe to Nanaimo, where they were employed on a road-building gang. They were paid for their work in blankets, which they traded in Victoria for a canoe. Then they traveled to Fort Rupert, where they were able to prove to the people of their own tribe that they had not been sorcerers by diving into a pit of hot water.

The people of Egulac were convinced, and the two men returned to their village to live.

This story is told by George Clutesi and recorded by John R. Swanton in 1911. It is one of the few myths to come from the Nanaimo dialect of the Hul'qui'nume language.

This is a story from the Kwakwaka'wakw people of the Pacific Northwest. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The story was recorded by ethnologist Franz Boas in 1905.

Analysis
The story is an example of a "supernatural helper" myth.  The spirit of the waterfall acts as a helper figure for Kwatlekwan, providing him with valuable information and aiding him in his pursuit of Tzeenaht.  The myth also contains elements of a vision quest, as Kwatlekwan and Tzeenaht go down to the river to hunt seals, but end up having a vision instead.

They heard a sound like the sound of a seal but it was too large to be a seal. It was the sound of a whale. They were afraid to return home without seals so they paddled out to the sound. They paddled for two hours and the sound became louder and louder until they were in the middle of a large bay. The fog was so thick that they could not see the shore. The sound of the whale was so loud that they could hear it cough. They heard the whale cough three times. They decided to follow the whale. They paddled for two hours and the whale coughed again. They paddled for another hour and the whale coughed a third time. They realized that the whale was guiding them. They paddled for another hour until they saw a light up ahead. They paddled towards the light and found themselves at a village where they were welcomed and given food. They later learned that the light was from a church and the village was the home of the people who had built the canoe they used to hunt seals. The whale was a humpback whale that was guiding them to safety.

The story also shows that the Tlingit people believed that whales were protectors who would guide humans to safety.

Interpretation
This story is about the power of the spirits and how they can be helpful to humans. The spirits give the two men food and improve their lives. The spirits are mysterious and have their own ways of communicating, but they are ultimately benevolent.

The source of the story mentioned that the two young men were out hunting seals, and seals are associated with the Underwater Panther, a creature that can bring good luck. The story also mentions the Chief of the Night, which is associated with the Underwater Chief, another creature that brings good luck. The canoe that the spirits sent is also associated with the Underwater Panther and the Underwater Chief.

Compare
This story is similar to the story of the Potlatch canoe. In both stories, spirits give humans a canoe filled with food. Suddenly a large, bright, circular object, like a full moon but brighter, descended from the heavens and came down on the river right in front of them.  It was so bright that it lit up the entire river and its surroundings.  One of the young men picked up a rock and threw it at the object, but it didn't make a dent.  Then the other young man picked up a stick and hit the object with it, and the stick broke in half.  The object started to spin around and as it was spinning, it started to move towards the ground.  When it reached the ground, it broke into three pieces, which became three stars in the sky.  These stars formed a constellation called "The Dipper" by the Cree people.  This constellation is also known as "The Great Bear" by other groups, including the English.

Origin
This legend is one of many stories that attempt to explain the creation of the Dipper constellation.  Many different versions of this story exist, each with slight variations in the details.  However, all of them share the same basic elements: a celestial object appears, the people try to destroy it, and it eventually becomes the Dipper constellation.

Meaning
This story is one of many that show how powerful and awe-inspiring the natural world is to indigenous peoples.  The people in this story are hunters, living off of the land and water.  They are so caught up in their hunting that they don't pay attention to the world around them.  They are startled by the sudden appearance of a bright, mysterious object, and they react with fear by trying to destroy it.  The object, however, is not destroyed.  Instead, it becomes a part of the natural world, a constellation in the sky.  This shows that while the people may think they are in control and can destroy whatever they want, there are forces at work that are much greater and more powerful than they are.

Moral/Lesson
This story shows how the natural world is powerful and awe-inspiring.  It also shows that people should pay attention to the world around them and not take it for granted.

The two men heard a voice calling them. They called back, "We are here, where are you?" The voice called again, "We are near you, but cannot come further." They called back, "Why is that?" The voice replied, "We are trapped by a great rock that has fallen from the sky." They asked where they were and the voice said, "We are near you, at the head of the lake." They went to the place where they heard the voice and there they found two young men trapped by a large boulder. The two Egulac young men tried to lift the rock but could not. The two trapped men told them to go and get help. So they left and went to the village and told everyone what had happened. Many people went back with them and they were all able to lift the rock and free the two men.

The two men who had been freed were very happy and they said to the Egulac men, "We want to thank you for helping us. We are the Two-headed Serpent, the guardians of this place. We are the guardians of the head of the lake. We will give you a gift to show our gratitude." They gave each of the Egulac men a beautiful stone. The Egulac people were very happy and they knew that they had been blessed.

The Two-headed Serpent is a guardian spirit who helps people who are trapped.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the sound of a man running with his arms stretched out to the sides, and they thought that it was a man running in the water and coming towards them.  Then they saw a light and heard a voice calling to them.  It was an Otter Spirits.  The Otter Spirit told them that they were the only two young men in the world and that they were to be the parents of many children and to live a long life, and then they would die and be transformed into Otters.  Then the Otter Spirit went back into the water and disappeared.  The two young men went back to their village and told the people what had happened to them.  Then they went to sleep and in the morning they had forgotten all about it.  Then, when they were 40 years old, they were called up again and the same thing happened to them.  Then they lived to be 100 years old and died, and their bodies were transformed into Otters.  And so they lived for many thousands of years.

This myth is from the Nuu-chah-nulth people of western Vancouver Island.  The Otter Spirit is one of many spirit helpers that appear in Nuu-chah-nulth myths.  The story seems to be saying that the Otter Spirit is a powerful being who can give immortality to humans, but only for a very long and tedious life.  The number 40 also appears in other myths, and seems to be a significant number.  The transformation of humans into animals is also common in Nuu-chah-nulth myths, and is usually a good thing.

They saw a light in the distance and thought it was a fishing village, but as they came closer they could see that the light was coming from a large canoe with many people in it. The canoe was coming toward them and they could see that the people in the canoe were coming to take them.
The people in the canoe were Kwakiutl, or as they called themselves, Kwaguilth. They took the two young men back with them to their village. The young men stayed with them for a while, then they returned to Egulac.
Soon after this, a great many Kwakiutl came to Egulac in their canoes. They traded goods with the people of Egulac and then they took some of the Egulac people back with them to their village.
This went on for some time, until one year when a smallpox epidemic broke out in the Kwakiutl villages. The people of Egulac knew that they must avoid the Kwakiutl until the smallpox was gone, so they built a high fence across the sandbar that connected their island to the mainland.
When the Kwakiutl came with their canoes to trade, the people of Egulac would not come out. The Kwakiutl tried to trade with the people of Egulac by throwing goods over the fence, but the people of Egulac would not take the goods.
The Kwakiutl were angry with the people of Egulac for refusing to trade with them, so they went away and never returned. From then on the people of Egulac lived in peace, but they were cut off from the outside world until one day, many years later, a trader came to their village and brought them news of many new things that were happening in the world outside.

Suddenly they heard a sound like the roar of a bear, then another and another.  They tried to run but the sound of bears roaring was all around them.  They tried to hide but where they hid was not good enough and they were chased by the bears.  They climbed up the cliffs to escape but the bears climbed the cliffs too.  The young men were scared and didn't know what to do.  Then they saw a raven standing on a rock and they knew that the raven was their friend.  The raven spoke to them and told them what to do.

The raven was Coyote and he was the trickster of the First People.  He helped the two young men get away from the bears.  He made the bears sleep and then he made them go away.  The two young men were very grateful to Coyote for saving their lives.  They thanked him and asked him why he had helped them.  Coyote said that he had heard them talking about him and how he was not as good as the other animals.  He had come to show them that he was just as good as any of them and that he could help them when they were in trouble.  He told them that they should never think badly of him again.

The two young men went back to their village and told everyone what had happened.  From then on they never spoke badly of Coyote again.  They respected him and they were friends with him.  They told their children and their children's children to do the same.  And so Coyote became a teacher and a helper of the First People.

This story is told by the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest.  It is a story about how Coyote became the trickster of the animals.  Coyote is found all over North America but the Tlingit call him Gyanout.  He is a trickster and he is known for his cunning and his ability to get out of bad situations.  This story shows how Coyote helps two young men escape from bears and how he teaches them a lesson.  It is a reminder to always respect Coyote and to never think badly of him.  This story is part of the oral tradition of the Tlingit people and it is still told today.

They heard a sound coming from the water. One of them said, "I think it is a canoe." But the other one said, "I think it is a bear." They argued about it for a while and then they decided to run. As they were running, they heard the sound again and they saw a light behind them. They looked back and saw a canoe heading towards them. They kept running until they got to a hill and looked back and saw that the canoe had gone. They went back to their camp and told their chief what had happened. The chief said, "Tomorrow we will go to where you saw the light and we will take the canoe away from there."
The men of the village went to the place where the two young men had seen the light and they found a canoe stuck in the mud. They tried to move it and they couldn't. They tried to pull it apart and they couldn't. Finally, after trying for a long time, they were able to move it. They took it to the top of the hill and they burned it. When they had finished, they went home.
The next day, the two young men were out hunting again and they saw a canoe at the edge of the water. They saw a man sitting in the canoe and he was singing. They went closer and they saw that the man was singing a song about a canoe getting stuck in the mud. They asked him where he was from and he said he was from a place far away. They asked him how he had gotten there and he said that he had been blown there by the wind. They looked at the canoe and they saw that there were no poles or sail. They looked at each other and they knew that it was the canoe that they had burned on the hill. The man sang his song and then he went away. The two young men went back to their camp and they told their chief what had happened. The chief said, "I know that song. It is a song that comes from a long way away. It is a song that comes from a place where there are no poles or sail. It is a song that comes from a place where there is no wind."

Suddenly they heard a sound like the noise of a waterfall and then they heard a voice singing.  They called out and the voice answered.  They asked who was singing and a woman called back. They asked where she was and she told them she was sitting in a canoe at the end of the shore.  They asked what she was doing there and she told them she was watching for the dawn.  They asked if it was dawn yet and she told them no, but that it would be soon.  They asked if they could see her and she told them no, but that she would sing for them.  She sang and then asked them if they were brothers.  They told her no, but that they were inseparable.  She told them that was enough for her and she would sing for them again.  She sang and then asked if they were in love.  They told her yes, and she told them that she loved them too.  She asked if they would give their names and they told her.  She told them that she would remember them and then she sang again.  She asked where they lived and they told her.  She told them that she would visit them in their dreams and sing to them.  She told them to look for her there and she sang once more.  Then she told them goodbye and they heard the sound of a canoe leaving.  They looked for her but she was gone.  They looked at each other and then they saw that it was dawn.

Suddenly a great wave arose and swamped them; they were unable to reach the shore. The wave had been produced by a supernatural being, a sea otter, who had been angered by their hunting. The two young men cried out for help and the sea otter came and lifted them onto its back. It then dived and swam around for a while before bringing them back to the shore. The young men were frightened and begged the sea otter to release them, but it refused, saying that it intended to keep them with it.
As they were traveling along the coast, the sea otter met a young woman who was collecting shellfish. The otter told her that it was taking the two young men to its house. She agreed to go with them and they all swam to the place where the otter's house was hidden, underground. It had a large entrance with wooden bars over it, and inside there were many other people. The young men and the woman were astonished and wondered where they all came from. The otter told them that they were all the children of people who had been drowned by the sea otter and his wife.
The three of them stayed with the sea otter for three years. The woman became the wife of one of the young men and they lived happily.
